10.2d — Turn Logic: Selection + Iteration

The starter's other empty method: AI_Turn(). Your opponent's brain. Today you build an AI that reads a list, makes a decision, and takes its turn — the exam's algorithm requirements (sequencing + selection + iteration) assembled into one method you can point to on the exam as YOURS.

Concept Lab ~10 min

What does an AI turn DO? Read the starter's partially-implemented Deal() and your 10.2c draw; the AI's turn is a decision on top of the same lists. Design the three layers before coding:

  1. Traverse the AI's hand (iteration)
  2. Score each card by your game's rules (selection: which is playable? which is best?)
  3. Play one: remove from hand, resolve its effect, end turn (sequencing)

That is literally the exam's algorithm definition wearing a hat — and it is why this method is the Create PT's best friend: a list, a procedure with parameters, a decision loop, a call.

Socratic

"AI" in your game is a set of IF statements — no learning, no mystery. Why is that honest design for a card game (what does the player actually want from a jam opponent — cleverness, or READABLE rules)? Where would REAL machine learning belong instead (9.6a — and whose data would it learn from)?

Build Lab ~35 min

Step 1 — the greedy AI (20 min). Fill AI_Turn() in the starter's voice:

public void AI_Turn()
{
    Card bestCard = null;
    int bestScore = -1;

    foreach (Card c in aiHand)              // ITERATION
    {
        if (c.cost <= aiEnergy)              // SELECTION: playable?
        {
            int score = c.attack * 2 + c.defense;
            if (score > bestScore)           // SELECTION: best?
            {
                bestScore = score;
                bestCard = c;
            }
        }
    }

    if (bestCard != null)                   // SELECTION: can we play?
    {
        aiHand.Remove(bestCard);
        PlayCard(bestCard, owner: AI);      // your resolve procedure
    }
    else
    {
        Pass();
    }
    EndTurn();
}

Read it aloud: traverse, filter, compare, act, or pass. The null check at the end is the same guard-clause religion as the empty deck (10.2c) — an AI with NOTHING playable must pass, not crash.

Step 2 — the turn loop. Whose turn is it? One bool (playerTurn) flipped by EndTurn(), with player input gated behind it — the turret's cooldown pattern (3.3a) repurposed as a STATE GATE. Trace one full round on paper: player draws (Deal), plays, ends turn → bool flips → AI_Turn() runs → bool flips back.

Step 3 — a 1.0s pause for the AI turn. The AI playing instantly feels like a bug to players. A simple coroutine or a timer (3.3a timestamps!) before AI_Turn() runs gives the game the rhythm of an opponent. Feel is not decoration — it is legibility.

Bug Hunt: AI bugs

  1. The AI plays its best card EVERY turn and always wins. Your game has a balance bug or an AI bug — which, and what single number would you change to test which one it is?
  2. The AI plays TWO cards in one turn. Where did the gate fail — and why is "one action per turn" a STATE question, not an IF question?
  3. Best card score ties (two cards score 9). Which does your foreach pick, and why is "first found wins" actually FINE (what does determinism buy a tester)?
  4. The player's turn triggers while AI_Turn() is still resolving. Draw the timeline of the bool flips — which flip came EARLY, and which line must move?
Close of Day ~5 min

Tinker: AI personality

  1. Give the AI a PERSONALITY by changing the score line: aggressive (attack × 3), defensive (defense × 3 + heal bonus). Play each — can a tester tell the difference blind? That is your 9.5a experiment design muscle, in a jam.
  2. Commit + push: "10.2d: AI_Turn implemented + turn gate".

Checkpoint — before moving on, you must be able to:

  • Implement a greedy AI: traverse, filter, compare, act/pass
  • Explain the turn loop as a bool state gate
  • Label sequencing/selection/iteration inside AI_Turn on sight
  • Give an AI personality via one score line
